newsitem.title: FRANCE: French jobless falls in March on way into election.
newsitem.headline: French jobless falls in March on way into election.

text.p: French unemployment, a major blot on the centre-right government's record, fell by 4,800 in March, less than a month ahead of a parliamentary election, the labour ministry said on Wednesday.
Wednesday's jobless data are the last ones before the two-round election on May 25 and June 1.

The number of jobless fell a seasonally adjusted 0.2 percent to 3,087,500. But the unemployment rate, calculated on the basis of different International Labour Organisation (ILO) criteria, stayed at a record 12.8 percent which it hit in February.

"The fall is most marked for young people less than 25 years old, where the fall was 7,600, or 1.3 percent, with the decline especially among young men, at 1.8 percent," the ministry said in a statement.
Economists said the latest figure would be good news for the ruling centre-right coalition but several were sceptical about data issued so soon before an election.
The ministry said unemployment at the end of March was 0.2 percent lower than in February and 2.2 percent higher than at the same stage a year earlier.
But the number out of work when based in ILO measures was 0.2 percent higher than at the end of February and 4.6 percent up year-on-year.
The labour ministry said unemployment among men and women of less than 25 years of age fell by 585,500.
March saw a rise in the number of long-term unemployed, with those out of work for a year or more rising 0.2 percent in March to more than 1.1 million. They account for one in three jobless.

The immediate reaction from economic experts was that this was good for the government, but that not too much should be read into the figures, and they highlighted differences between the number of unemployed according to national or ILO criteria.

"In an electoral campaign environment these figures have to be taken with a pinch of salt. It looks like unemployment data is not meant to interfere with the campaign," said JP Morgan economist David Naude. "Needless to say in the current environment these figures are of little informative value."

"It's not quite as stark as in the U.K. (Britain) but it's the same situation in that the headline numbers are not behaving in the same way as the ILO numbers. It's clear the labour market in France is still pretty soft," said Sean Shepley, economist at CS First Boston.

Shepley was referring to criticism by many analysts that extensive changes to the way British jobless totals are measured mean that monthly figures greatly exaggerate the health of the British economy.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe's ruling coalition promised a war against unemployment after Conservative President Jacques Chirac came to power in May 1995 on a campaign pledge to make this a top priority, but has been blighted by the vow ever since.
But Juppe and Finance Minister Jean Arthuis both said on Tuesday that unemployment had stabilised and would start to turn down later this year and in 1998.

The European Commission said last week it was forecasting French unemployment of 12.5 percent for 1997 and 12.1 percent unemployment in 1998. The International Monetary Fund said last week it was predicting French unemployment at 12.8 percent this year and 12.3 percent next year.
